utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Kuzmanovic, I was informed that you would like to address the Chamber in relation to the disclosure issue you raised yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Your Honour. Mr. Waespi and I talked this morning briefly. I wanted to make the Chamber aware that we did endeavour to begin to looking at the documents that were disclosed to us the other morning, early in the morning. There are roughly 3.000 pages' worth of materials. Of those 3.000 pages, 1100 pages were documents that were not previously disclosed to us and which we didn't have in our system. So, as the Chamber is obviously aware, that is a lot to go through. I was up till about 2.30 last night, plowing through some of it. In light of that, we would request, in terms of the proposal that was discussed yesterday, that with respect to these documents not previously disclosed, and Mr. Waespi advises this morning there is an additional much smaller disclosure of but of one document for which they're waiting Rule 70 authority, that we would be allowed to meet with the witness to discuss these documents only, after the witness is sworn and testifies, because I think that is going to be necessary under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. The good news is first two things. We just checked in relation to that key document that we have received Rule 70 clearance in -- in another case, and I think that is safe to give it to you. I have a hard copy here - I think it is an important document - so it can be given to the witness. And it's correct that we have finished the review now, so that's the good news. And as I said, there are 29 English documents, mostly open sources, BBC, Reuters, which we'll give you if our check reveals that it has not been disclosed, and also 175 B/C/S documents, again, mostly B/C/S sources. We will review whether it has been disclosed. If not, you will get it certainly today. That's the status of disclosure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So I do understand with that, Mr. Kuzmanovic, although with great hesitation you are willing to start examination-in-chief of the next witness but that you feel only able to do so if you would have an opportunity to speak with the witness in between about newly disclosed documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's on the record. Thank you very much. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In order to speed up the process, I can give the hard copy to -- to Mr. Kuzmanovic of that one document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is two very, not necessarily minor, but issues that I would like to raise with the Chamber - thank you - with respect to the next witness and -- or the current witness, and there are not going to be any specifics but I think we should go into private session for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Mikulicic, you said errare humanum est. I immediately wanted to underline by forgetting to give an instruction to the witness. So I fully agree with you. The parties are hereby informed that I asked Mr. Registrar, within five seconds after that, to give the instruction to the witness. We move into closed session to continue hearing the evidence of the witness who took the stand yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. We'll have a break, and we will resume at 20 minutes past 11.00, and we'll then continue in open session --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Next witness is here and should be ready, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So we'll -- then you'll start your examination after the break. As I said, 20 minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since there are no preliminary matters to be raised, I would ask Madam Usher to escort the witness into the courtroom. The already admitted statements of Witnesses IC-12 and IC-16 have now been uploaded in the way required by the Chamber. The only thing that has to be done is that a number should be assigned to them. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 2D00793, which is 65 ter for Witness IC-16's statement, that becomes Exhibit D1795. And then 65 ter 2D00794, which is the statement of IC-12, becomes Exhibit D1796.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it's -- it is confirmed that they have been uploaded, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, Your Honour. And also the order that you made in respect to the redaction, that was completed too. So I'm obliged to you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So then D1795 and D1796 are admitted into evidence. My apologies to you, Mr. Granic, for dealing with other matters while you entered the courtroom. Before you give evidence, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you, and I would like to invite to you make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Granic. Mr. Granic, you will first be examined by Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Mikulicic is counsel for Mr. Markac. Please proceed, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Granic.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC
utterances.text: Mate Granic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And what is your current profession?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC
utterances.text: I am currently the head of the high journalistic school and also the owner of a private consultant firm, Magra.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the name of your consultancy firm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It's correctly in the transcript, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then there is no need to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would ask the Registrar for the document 65 ter 3D00958.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, we will soon see on the screen a document which is actually your statement, so I will ask you a few questions about the statement which you gave to the Markac Defence team. So, Mr. Markac [as interpreted], do you remember that you gave a statement to the Defence of General Markac?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC
utterances.text: I remember that I gave a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And now when you see it on the screen, can you recognise your signature in the Croatian version of the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would ask the Registrar to scroll up the document a little bit. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature, Mr. Granic?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that you gave this statement at the premises in Zagreb on the 19th of May, 2009, to the Defence of General Markac?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to review and have a look at this statement after that, before coming to testify here?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had the opportunity to do that, and this is the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Does this statement correctly reflect what you said to the General Markac Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC
utterances.text: Absolutely correctly, and there is nothing I wish to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: While giving the statement, did you speak the truth, to the best of your knowledge and recollection, and has it been recorded in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC
utterances.text: Yes, everything is absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If the same questions were put to you today, as the ones you were asked when you were giving the statement, would you provide the same answers relating to the facts?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I ask for the statement to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just a point of clarification. I now have three dates for the witness statement. In the transcript it says the 19th of May, 2009. The English translation, at least the one I have now, has 12th of May. And I think the B/C/S has 11th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Obviously in the transcript there was a wrong translation, because I have in front me a Croatian version, the original version of the statement, which is dated 12th of May, 2009.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whereas apparently the English translation says the 11th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Well, it is a typo, obviously, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do not know exactly what happens at this moment. I'm not even aware on who prepared these translations. But this morning we had the issue of Croats and Serbs being mixed up in one of the documents. And I would still --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... official translation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Nevertheless, I express my concern without looking at anyone, but my main concern is that we have the proper translations. Mr. Mikulicic, would you take care that the document we saw this morning will be sent to be -- perhaps to be reviewed. We do not know whether it is just that one mistake which we were able to identify, and that is, of course, here the same. We can identify there is apparently a problem with the dates here. What other problems there are, I am unable to look at. So, therefore, if we find clear mistakes I would like to have them at least reviewed, if only superficially, that we do not have problems elsewhere. Mr. Mikulicic --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for your information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will do so. Just for your information the document we referred to this morning, our draft translation was correct. So it is somehow in the -- when it got to CLSS it got changed, so we will again double-check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so. Mr. Granic, I apologise for this. Apart from the date, Mr. Waespi --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1797.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1797 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Granic, please be so kind and tell us in several sentences --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But before we begin I prepared for this witness, for Mr. Granic, a folder with documents which are marked so that I could refer to specific documents during my questioning so that Mr. Granic could also see the hard copy of these documents. So, with you're allowance, this is what I would like to use during the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Leave is granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Granic, very briefly, can you tell us something about your education and your profession until the moment when you entered politics.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC
utterances.text: Before I became involved in politics, and that was in 1991, on the 3rd of August, I had a successful medical career. I was a professor of internal medicine, and I was also the deputy director and chief of the clinical department at the Institute of Diabetes, Endocrinology and Disease of the Metabolism, Vuk Vrhovac. I was a short-term consultant for the World Health Organisation in Asia, in India, Burma, Bangladesh, and Thailand. I was also a visiting researcher and a visiting professor in the USA, in Lexington, Kentucky. And I taught on -- around 17 American universities. I also took some training at Harvard Medical School and at the Munich University.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And after that, in 1990, as the summit of your medical career, you became the dean of the medical faculty of the university in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC
utterances.text: Correct. In 1989, I became the deputy dean, and in the fall of 1990, after the first free democratic elections, I became the dean of the medical faculty of the University of Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, just for your information, the pauses which I am making are motivated by allowing the interpreters to do their work, so I will ask you to wait for a short while with your answer after I ask a question. What was the motivation, Mr. Granic, to neglect a successful medical career and to decide to enter politics?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC
utterances.text: The motivation was just one. I decided to become involved with the democratic changes, and that was in late 1988, when I became a member of the alternative commission for the constitution. After the democratic changes, as a respected doctor and dean of the medical faculty, I became a member of the constitutional commission which was established by the president, Franjo Tudjman, but I didn't have any ambition at the time to enter politics. However, the aggression against my country and the danger for Croatia that was posed by the possibility that a Greater Serbia might be formed, and I was well-informed about what was going on in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. Croatia was under direct threat, and after three days of deliberation, when the prime minister designate, Franjo Gregoric and President Gregoric [as interpreted], offered that I enter the government as the deputy prime minister, I accepted that because I believed that, with my knowledge and experience, I could help. In particular, in the field that I was especially qualified, and I became the deputy prime minister for science, the education system, the health system, the social care system, and that was why I accepted to join the Croatian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If we divided your political engagement in the Croatian government into two stages, then the first one would be the one you just told us about. Can you tell us, as the deputy prime minister, what was your area of responsibility in practice? What was the main field of your work, what were your main tasks in the government of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC
utterances.text: Well, this government, this so-called government of democratic unity which all political forces in Croatia entered or supported it, once we began working then we could see that we did not even have the legal foundation for our work. So within a framework of 10 to 13 days, we had to adopt 79 decree laws so that we could operate successfully as the government. And after that, I saw that the chief problem was the mounting number of expelled persons. The number really grew rapidly, and I realised that my main task would be to care for the displaced persons and victims of the war. Therefore, I established the government office for displaced persons and refugees, and during the wars in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, it took care of a total of more than 700.000, between 700.000 and 800.000 displaced persons and almost 1 million refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina passed through this office. The biggest numbers of expelled persons at one moment was 485.000, and that was in late 1991 and early 1992. That was the biggest number of displaced persons. And the biggest number of refugees at one point was 325.000 from Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that was in early 1993. We should note that these are such huge figures that, on two occasions, more than 10.000 people came to the city of Zagreb in one day, especially after the fall of Vukovar, and on four occasions this figure was 5.000 people. And as for refugees, one should take note that during two weekends, the first weekend was in late May 1991, and the other weekend was between the 11th and 13th of July in 1992, during these weekends, 60.000 refugees entered Croatia on each of those two weekends. I also have to say another thing. We -- if we had established this office at the moment when the number mounted from one day to the next and when we were not receiving any international aid, except that received from the Croatian diaspora and the friendly towns and cities from neighbouring countries, we established this office with the help of UNHCR and practically we had excellent cooperation with them from beginning to the end, especially with Ms. Sagato Ogata, but also those who were the representatives for Croatia. Organised aid from the German government arrived for Christmas in 1991, and after Germany [as interpreted] was internationally recognised, then we also received aid from the European Union in early 1992. We received lots of aid from the neighbouring countries, that was Austria, Hungary, Slovakia, but also Switzerland and Germany.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think just in terms of the interpretation, I don't think there's going to be any dispute that at page 53, lines 9 and 10, it refers to Germany's recognition of Croatia and not Germany's international recognition of -- in other words, it says: "... and after Germany was internationally recognised ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, not Germany was but it was Croatia which was recognised by Germany. That seems to be clear. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, the Republic of Croatia and you, as the person who was charged with this particular task, were faced with a huge humanitarian effort. And how did it reflect itself on financial terms?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC
utterances.text: It was an enormous cost for the state, and a relief toward that cost came from the Croatian diaspora and the friendly towns that I mentioned. Nevertheless, it was an enormous burden upon the Croatian budget, especially in view of the fact that Croatia had at the same time been exposed to a forceful aggression from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the so-called former Yugoslav People's Army that was an instrument in the hands of Slobodan Milosevic. Another matter that I dealt with as a member of the government was that all of the victims of the war, all the captured soldiers of the former JNA had immediately been released through the Red Cross, and the number involved was at least 17.000. They were provided immediate relief and were immediately enabled to reunite with their families and go home. Another matter that was important for that period. On the 8th of October, 1991, I was appointed, by President Tudjman and the Croatian government, the chief negotiator with the former Yugoslav Army on the issue of the deblocking and evacuation of the barracks. On the 8th of December, 1991, after two months of negotiations, I brought the negotiations to a close with the Dutch ambassador, van Houten, and the American ambassador, Okun, or the American envoy Okun, and Admiral Raseta, by signing an agreement with them at the level of Croatia, although there were local negotiations taking place at the time, especially the ones led by Mr. Hebrang at the time, concerning a military hospital. This was a success on our part and the agreement was successfully implemented. The international community did not have any objections to make with regard to the implementation of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Already at this stage, Dr. Granic, we were able to see that you moved out of the refugee issues toward the task of negotiating with the Yugoslav People's Army. At the close of these negotiations, what were your next tasks within the government on this same issue?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC
utterances.text: The conditions for the international commission of Croatia that had been agreed upon at the meeting of EU ministers, on the night between 16th and 17th of December, with special engagement of the German foreign minister and German politicians Genscher and Kohl, it was agreed that Croatia should adopt a constitutional law on the protection of minorities. It should make sure that the barracks were deblocked and evacuated. A truce agreement was to be signed, which was, in fact, signed by -- on -- by Minister Susak on the 3rd of January, 1992, and the European observers who were in Zagreb were supposed to give a positive view on it. All these conditions were met, and on the 15th of January, Croatia was in fact recognised by the international community. Now, going back to the question of what I personally did at the time, I predominantly dealt with refugee issues, with the issue of exchanging prisoners and providing for the victims of war. In addition to all the other regular duties I had as the deputy prime minister for the social portfolio, which included negotiations with trade unions, et cetera, that -- those were my main tasks in the first half of 1992, as well as throughout 1992, although I was increasingly developing the so-called humanitarian diplomacy since we cooperated and dealt with almost all the United Nations specialised agencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, in the multitude of displaced persons, refugees, expelled persons, there were individuals of various ethnicities. Did you ever run any sort of policy that would favour one group over the other, among the multitude of the victims of war?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC
utterances.text: Absolutely not. Let me state that of -- even among the displaced persons, 3 per cent were Serbs, and this is not a fact well known. As for the refugees, the vast majority were Bosniaks. There had never been any serious incident there, even though it was far from easy to deal with such a throng of people. When you compare it with some other large countries, this was an enormous number of people for Croatia, which was a country of 4 million people, and even fewer people, since a third of the country was occupied. In other words, this was an enormous number of people which practically claimed 10 per cent of the state budget in order for us to be able to provide care for all of victims of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Following the international recognition of Croatia which you have just described, there followed a period, where, in fact, in the territory of the Republic of Croatia an undeclared war was waged. Moreover, the war spilled over to the territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I should first note that, together with President Tudjman, I took part in the talks concerning the deployment of UN peacekeeping forces to Croatia with the state secretary Vance. The -- Croatia was strongly in favour of this agreement which local rebel Serbs rejected. This was one of the tasks that I performed. As for Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatia supported the referendum for independence and was the first to dispatch its ambassador to Sarajevo. It was quite clear that a war was brewing in Bosnia-Herzegovina. There was hardly a single representative of the international community whom I didn't discuss this issue with. It was very unfortunate that the international community was unable to muster strength or at least find a negotiator in order to bring about a consensus on the issue in the face of this threat of a war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, to avert the aggression forged by Slobodan Milosevic, to be carried out also against Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In this second stage of your activity, as it were, the primary task was to avert a war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. What was your attitude toward these activities; and what was exactly the job you did at the time?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC
utterances.text: Up until the 1st of June, 1993, my primary concern were refugees, displaced persons, and victims of war. We had, I believe, two or three shelters for women victims of rape from Bosnia-Herzegovina that we set up with the considerable assistance from the international community. That was my primary concern. At the time, I did not participate in the political talks over peace in Bosnia and Herzegovina, so I am not your best witness for the negotiations concerning the restoration of peace or preservation of peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, when I became foreign minister, because of the unfortunate conflict between Croats and Bosniaks, the -- the international position and reputation of Croatia was greatly undermined. In my discussions with Madam Albright, who was a representative of the US in the United Nations in New York at the time, and Klaus Kinkel, the German foreign minister, Jean Leuterand [phoen], or the person who became in charge of relations with the individual who was there on -- on behalf of the Vatican, the Italian foreign minister, all these discussions had the result of me actually being involved in those months in the effort to stop the conflict between Bosniaks and Croats in Bosnia, and forging their alliance. This was something that the international credibility of Croatia definitely depended on, and most of my efforts were engaged in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you please set a time on these events you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the period starting from the 1st of June, 1993, when I became minister, through to the end of the year, and the Washington Agreement. In addition to the care for refugees, this was one of the most important tasks I performed in my life. I also have to state that I faced this cruel reality, where sometime around the 16th or 17th of June, 1993, I was foreign minister and I was informed one morning by the spokesperson that the "New York Times" and another paper, I think "Le Monde", but definitely the "New York Times," wrote an article stating that the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina had collection centres or camps where civilians were held. I was shocked by the news. I rang Mate Boban right away and asked him if it was true. He said that it was not. I then asked Mr. Jadranko Prlic if this was indeed true and he confirmed that it was indeed true that there was a collection centre, and I heard only of this one in that instance. I phoned Boban again and I strongly protested. I almost shouted at him. I called President Tudjman and informed him of it. He gave his full support and told me that I do everything in my power to press the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina into closing the collection centre, and this was to be done unilaterally, without waiting for any sort of bilateral agreements. Twenty days later, I organised a meeting in Makarska, attended by the highest representative of the government at the level of the deputy prime minister of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the BiH army, HVO, the Croatian Defence Council, and representative of the ICRC and the High Commissioner, where the following was agreed. The Makarska Declaration was signed, whereby free passage was to be ensured for all convoys and where by all the detainees, all the prisoners were to be released.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let us return to the topic which you touched on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the meantime if we could please see 3D00464.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Granic, it is tab 1 in your folder. It is undoubted that the issue of relations between the Republic of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina was of utmost importance, as said yourself, and I will ask you to focus your attention on 1992, when the president of the Republic of Croatia and the president of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Dr. Tudjman and Mr. Alija Izetbegovic signed an appendix to earlier Agreement on Friendship and Cooperation. As the deputy prime minister at the time, did you know about this agreement and this importance? Can you please comment on this document.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC
utterances.text: This is the addendum to the agreement which was signed in early July; I think it was the 11th of July, 1992. And on the basis of it, the Croatian army could enter to up to 20 kilometres within the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, because aggression against Croatia had already been carried out by Croatian Serbs from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. They had destroyed the Croatian village of Ravno, and this was the addendum to the agreement that was signed in New York City during the UN General Assembly. I think that that was when the meeting took place. I have to note that the real negotiations about stopping the conflict between the Croats and Bosniaks were started by Mr. Haris Silajdzic, who was firstly the minister and then the foreign -- firstly the foreign minister and then the prime minister of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In the month of August 1993, for seven days we met every day. The last day, that was together with President Tudjman, and that was when it de facto agreed that several things would take place. One thing was that the war between the Croats and the Bosniaks would be stopped, that peace would be restored, that groups would be established to rebuild trust, that humanitarian issues needed to be resolved, and I have to note that the result was the signature in Geneva to the new agreement between Izetbegovic and Tudjman. That was on 16th September. Unfortunately, two days, later, Lord Owen organised a meeting of Bosniaks and Serbs who signed a similar agreement which, to a certain extent, annulled the effects of this agreement. This was a very difficult time, a time of conflict, and of negotiations but I was very persistent. I visited Sarajevo during the war. I signed the Sarajevo Declaration. And when the Vance-Owen Plan and then the Vance-Stoltenberg Plan did not work, it was obvious that European Community and the negotiators did not have enough strength to establish lasting peace. Lasting peace was established when the United States became involved. That implied the strong administration of the Bill Clinton. The first of the meetings was organised on the 16th or 17th of January, 1994, in Geneva. I do not remember the exact date, but Charles Redmond was present there. He was the special envoy of President Clinton. And Ambassador Zuzul was our ambassador in Geneva at the time, and I was there myself, and practically that was the moment when the concept about restoring peace and creating the federation of Croats and Bosniaks was decided, and this was completed with the negotiations in Washington. But before that, some other important things took place as the precondition for this agreement. Namely, the departure of Mate Boban and the group of people around him. They had left the political scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Granic, this document before you, the addendum to the agreement on the friendship, implicitly talks about the effort to find a political solution and to stop the war and to have a union, a joint effort of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Republic of Croatia in these efforts. Does the text of this agreement reflect the position of the government of the Republic of Croatia about finding peaceful solutions and finding resolution apart from the unnecessary problems that the war entailed? Can you please go back to tab 1.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was certainly so. I said that I'm not the best witness about all the negotiations that were conducted as part of the conference to establish peace in Bosnia and Herzegovina. But it is a fact that Croatia accepted Cutileiro's plan and supported it, that it accepted the Vance-Owen Plan and supported it, and so did the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It also accepted and supported the Vance-Owen Plan and the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document please be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1798.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Following the policy aimed at peaceful solution and adhering to international law relating to refugees, which we just saw, the president of the Republic, Dr. Franjo Tudjman, in late November 1994, gave a speech before the General Assembly of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would ask the Registry to show the document 3D00476. If we could please see page 9 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting, Dr. Granic, it is under tab 2 in your binder, page 9, the paragraph at the bottom of the page. While we are waiting for it to appear on the screen, were you present in New York, before the General Assembly, on this occasion when General Tudjman addressed the General Assembly by this speech in late 1994?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC
utterances.text: In 1994, absolutely, yes. And I remember well this speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, I will focus your attention to the last paragraph on page 9, where President Tudjman says that Croatia proposes the provision of a permanent peacekeeping force for intervention - I'm not reading directly this text; I'm just interpreting - in accordance with the requirements of the Security Council, and that the mandate of such forces should even include using force in order to implement their mandate and not just to protect themselves. My question is: What is your experience with the mandate that the international organisations, whether it was UNPROFOR or the European monitors, had in the territory of the Republic of Croatia? Was there an issue with the structure of the mandate as compared with the real needs on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC
utterances.text: We were happy about the arrival of peacekeeping forces, and we have to thank everyone who participated in this operation, and in particular, those who were -- gave their lives or who were wounded or who had any kind of problems during this operation. Finally, the peacekeeping forces helped Croatia to become a sovereign and territorially integrated country. However, it needs to be noted that the mandate of these forces was not clearly defined and that the peacekeeping forces did not manage to control the border between the Republic of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the consequence of that were the operations of the rebelled Croatian Serbs, the so-called Krajina, against the Bihac area. In addition to this, the peacekeeping forces never managed to disarm completely the local Serbs who had rebelled. During the UNPROFOR's mandate, the Croats and non-Serbs who were killed were between 6 and 700 in number, around 650, and a great number of people were expelled, practically ethnic cleansing was carried out. It's a historical fact. So regardless of the good intentions, and regardless of the commitment of many of these soldiers, these are the historical facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Granic, you mentioned the situation that - and we're talking about late 1994 - the situation in the territory of the Republic of Croatia at the time. We had this creation, the so-called Republic of Serbian Krajina, and how the rebelled Serbian citizens in the territory conducted themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we now move to page 16 of this document. I would ask the Registry to show that on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We will find a paragraph in which President Tudjman, in his speech, refers to this situation, and he says in the second paragraph: "We realise that both sides, after any conflict, have to invest much time and effort into restoring and strengthening mutual confidence. We are also quite aware that no long-term stability and progress is possible in Croatia without guaranteed human and ethnic rights to the Serbian and other minority groups. We have indeed guaranteed such rights by a special constitutional law ... but we urge the international community to create conditions for the implementation of this law in accordance with Security Council resolutions." Dr. Granic, this is the position of the president of the republic, Dr. Franjo Tudjman, before the General Assembly of the United Nations, in which he reflects the position of the Republic of Croatia towards the rebelled Serbs and also ethnic and minority rights. Please tell me, considering that you were in the government, you held the position of the foreign minister at the time, what was the state policy of the Republic of Croatia through the government and the policy of the president of Franjo Tudjman, and does this correspond with your experience and your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC
utterances.text: In 1994, several important things happened, and they all reflect the government policy of the Republic of Croatia. Firstly, I think it was on the 19th of January, in Geneva, an agreement was signed between Granic and Jovanovic. And this agreement was the first step by which Belgrade accepted that we should take serious steps and talk. It was not just that as the government we were conducting negotiations with the local Serbs, but that Belgrade also accepted that offices should be established in Zagreb and Belgrade so that we could communicate more easily, and that we should try to reach a peaceful resolution. After that, on the 3rd of March, 1994, the Washington Agreement was signed. That was the key agreement for the peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina, for stopping the war between the Croats and Bosniaks, and for the establishment of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that was done with the patronage of the United States. And on the Croatian side, I was the main negotiator. After that, I also visited Belgrade. I discussed with Deputy President Simic. He visited Zagreb, and in December of that year, an economic agreement was also signed with the local Serbs about opening up the highway, the oil pipeline, the power supply problems, and so on. The local Serbs accepted that, partly because they were under pressure of the international community, partly from Belgrade, to negotiate about economic issues. But never, absolutely never did they accept to talk about political issues and their reintegration in the state and legal system of Croatia. And in that year there is another fact which is historically important. In December of that year, the UN General Assembly adopted a resolution, that was 43/44, in which it was said that the UNPA territories were the occupied territories of the Republic of Croatia and that Belgrade was responsible for the situation and the ethnic cleansing in these areas. That is a very important document which was adopted by the UN General Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let us put it in a geographical context. When you said that the agreement was signed with the local Serbs on the opening up of the highway, which part of the Republic of Croatia did that concern?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC
utterances.text: The primary focus was on Sector West and the highway between Zagreb and Belgrade, as well as the oil pipeline which went through the sector, Sector North. We also discussed the opening up of the railway and all those elements of importance. There was, indeed, hope at the time that the issue of reintegration could be resolved peacefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Granic, what was the position of the Croatian government that were a part of as a foreign minister and deputy prime minister about minority issues and the protection of human rights as well as the principle of ethnic protection, primarily the Serbs who resided in the territory of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC
utterances.text: There were never any dilemmas or doubts about the fact that the Serbs were Croatian citizens and that they should enjoy the highest possible degree of protection in terms of their human, ethnic minority, cultural, and all other rights pursuant to the highest standard of European rights protection. There was never any discussion about that in Croatian government. There was never any doubt. However, one needs to mention that the core problem was that, on the one hand, the local rebelled Serbs, and I don't mean those Serbs residing in urban areas throughout the Republic of Croatia. Most of whom stayed. I have in mind the rebelled Serbs who were exposed to -- powerfully indoctrination for a number of years, and at least as of 1997, when Milosevic assumed power, their leadership practically rejected any kind of Croatian state. That was the main problem which, later on, resulted in the departure of those people after Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We are still to get to that topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the time being, I would seek to tender 3D00476.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1799.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the introductory part, we mentioned, Mr. Granic, the war in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina which posed a significant security threat. And we discussed the relationship between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, in terms of that war. Could we please look at another document. It is tab 3 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the Registrar to display 3D00475.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It is dated around mid-November 1994. To be more correct -- more precise, it was on the 12th of November. It was signed by Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, the then president of Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And he sent it to Dr. Franjo Tudjman, Croatian president. Implicitly what is mentioned is that there was a powerful attack on the protected area of Bihac, stating that the main direction of attack was from Croatia, primarily from the so-called UNPA areas. Mr. Izetbegovic says -- or, rather, invited Mr. Tudjman, in keeping with the spirit of provision of Article 8 on cooperation between the two countries and the agreement on friendship, that he should act in such a way that all measures be taken to prevent any such further attacks on Bosnia-Herzegovina from Croatian territory. Mr. Granic, what do you recall about this period?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC
utterances.text: I recall this period fully. On the 11th of November, 1994, I received a call from Mr. Sacirbey, who was the foreign minister, and told me that the situation was dramatic regarding Bihac. He was asking me to do everything possible to at least make the defence of Bihac more easy, because the focus of attacks was from the side of the rebelled Serbs, from the area where Martic was in power. That day, I had a meeting with the defence minister, Mr. Susak. We agreed that we should, together, propose to President Tudjman that Croatia break through, thus opening a 20-kilometre-wide corridor, to alleviate the situation in Bihac and to prevent its fall. We also agreed that we should consult with the American ambassador. We arranged a meeting with him. The ambassador was Mr. Peter Galbraith, who was delighted with the idea. However, he was supposed to seek advice from President Clinton and the State Department. Minister Susak and myself went to see Mr. Tudjman the next day. The prime minister, Mr. Valentic, was in attendance as well. We discussed the topic and the president, in principle, accepted our idea. He warned us, though, that this could mean the opening up of the entire front line, which, at that moment, Croatia was not ready. The preparations to liberate that territory by military means was not something that Croatia could undertake at that point in time. Although he did not completely refuse the idea of helping Bihac. We decided that we should wait for the American official position. On the 12th, Alija Izetbegovic also addressed President Tudjman on the issue, after which the American ambassador arrived, who informed us officially that it was the position of the American government that it will do its utmost through Security Council, but that, at that point in time, advised against any military operations. And President Tudjman, indeed, followed the American advice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I seek to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1800.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1800 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the Registrar for 3D00474.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we move to the next exhibit. I'm looking at the clock, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will complete it within two minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then we'll --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is tab 4, Mr. Granic, in your binder. You mentioned that you waited for the official position of the US regarding the Bihac issue. You mentioned that Mr. Galbraith arrived and said that they advised against that but, however, that they would try to act through the UN Security Council. Please have a look at this document of the 16th of November, 1994. It is a note of a discussion between Mr. Tudjman and the ambassador, Peter Galbraith. In the right-hand corner, I believe I recognise your signature.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You authored this document, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In it, you state that an urgent meeting of Security Council should be held, during which the US would seek to implement active measures to prevent the fall of Bihac and to stop any further aggression by the Bosnian and Krajina Serbs. Mr. Granic, the issue of Bihac, why was it of such importance at that point in time, and indeed it was so important that US intervention was sought through Security Council. Why was it such an important issue? If can you put it in a few sentences because we already heard some evidence about it.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC
utterances.text: The issue of Bihac was important because it may have resulted in mass crimes. Over 100.000 people were in encirclement, and had Bihac fallen, it would have been the greatest disaster in an already disastrous war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. On the other hand, Bihac was surrounded and attacked by both Karadzic and Mladic, that is to say, they -- their army, as well as by the army of Martic's Serbs. In other words, it was a joint operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I thank you for your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I think that's appropriate time for taking a break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will have a break, and we will resume at ten minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Your Honour, can we call up 65 ter document, 3D00474 -- or, rather, can we have it admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1801.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1801 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Granic, before the break, we discussed the situation in Bihac and the note you made during the talks between Ambassador Galbraith and President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we can call up 3D00471.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Which is T5 in your binder. Therefore, there are further developments to follow. President Tudjman, because of the situation in the Bihac/UN protected zone, addressed Madam Madeleine Albright who was the chairperson of the UN General Assembly. This was the 22nd of November, 1994. And if we look at President Tudjman's letter, we can see that she [as interpreted] draws the attention of Madam Albright to the situation in the protected area of Bihac and around it. The situation was further aggravated because of the Serb forces who, from the UNPA zones from Croatia, attacked this particular area. On the second page of this letter President Tudjman states: "For this reason, appeal to you as the president of the Security Council of the United Nations to take resolute measures to ensure that all UN resolutions be adopted that may ensure a lasting political solution to the crisis and a lasting peace in the region." Mr. Granic, as a minister of foreign affairs, were you aware of this letter by President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes. In fact, this was my proposal to President Tudjman, and the American ambassador was informed accordingly. We also informed President Izetbegovic and Minister Sacirbey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What was the reaction to the initiative?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC
utterances.text: We truly believed that the United States of America were doing everything to ensure a lasting peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and we took an active part in the process.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, can the document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1802.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1802 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Granic, we spoke of the role UNPROFOR played, and under the documents, it was supposed to be deployed to the borders of the Republic of Croatia. However, the situation developed differently than there was general discontents in the Republic of Croatia with regard to the role and activities of UNPROFOR. We are now in the first half of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can we call up 3D0047 -- 468 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Which is also to be found in your binder. There is a letter where President Tudjman addresses the General Secretary of the United Nations, Mr. Boutros-Ghali, dated the 12th of January, 1995. This is tab 6. In the letter he refers to the UNPROFOR mandate and the role it played. At page 2 of the letter, President Tudjman states that for the two years during which UNPROFOR was present in Croatia, the process of ethnic cleansing of Croats and non-Serbs in the occupied territories was completed. Before the arrival of UNPROFOR, the Serb rebels, with the assistance of the JNA, drove out and ethnically cleansed of the occupied territory 390.000 non-Serb citizens - these were Croats, Hungarians, Ruthenians, Czechs, Slovaks, et cetera - and killed several thousand of them in the process. Around 600 Croats were killed and 12.000 were forcibly removed ever since UNPROFOR was deployed to the area. By way of conclusion, the president, Tudjman, said that the Croatian parliament adopted a resolution on the 23rd of September, whereby it decided that the UN Protection Forces, that's to say UNPROFOR, no longer should have their term of office or mandate extended. Mr. Granic, from what you remember of UNPROFOR, its mandate and the issue of it being extended or not extended in the occupied territories, what can you tell us about it?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC
utterances.text: We simply did not want to have the mandate of UNPROFOR as it had been by that time anymore. It was the sort of mandate which served to freeze the state of affairs as it was, and the state of affairs was that Serbs were ethnically cleansing Croats. UNPROFOR did not control the border. The attacks on Bihac from the territory of the Republic of Croatia continued. UNPROFOR failed to disarm, in particular, of the heavy weaponry, which had been one of its major tasks. In addition, not even the economic agreement from December 1994, which had been signed, was being adhered to. By working toward the cancellation of the mandate as it was, Croatia did not want to cause a conflict with the United Nations. Quite the contrary. By raising the issue of the UNPROFOR's mandate, we opened a decision on the matter. Ultimately, with the assistance of the US, especially the state secretary, Christopher, Madeleine Albright, the representative in the United Nations, and Vice-President Al Gore, we managed to find a common language with the United Nations and bring about a new mandate of UNCRO, which applied to Croatia only and whose tasks were better defined. We believed that the new mandate with tasks that were closely defined would help implement what was, in fact, the basic task of the mandate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In that same letter addressed to Mr. Boutros-Ghali, and this is page 4 of the document, President Tudjman says that the Republic of Croatia remained true to its policy -- long-standing policy aimed towards the peaceful reintegration of the territory, and continued to offer all Croats in Croatia a cultural autonomy and the highest level of local autonomy in those areas and counties where the Serbs were in the majority, in accordance with the population census, with full respect of all human rights, especially the rights of minorities, this is the view which representatives of the international community can take into account. And this is what President Tudjman wrote in the letter. Was this the sort of position that reflected the state policy of the Republic of Croatia, one which you also presented?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. The position was to try at all costs to find a peaceful solution and to peacefully reintegrate the occupied areas into the state and legal system of Croatia. This position vis-a-vis UNPROFOR, which had been defined in the Croatian parliament and formulated in the letter by President Tudjman to Secretary-General of the United Nations, did in fact yield definite results because the international community, following the letter, started working intensely on the so-called Z-4 plan. This was the first time that the international community worked on a plan that envisaged a peaceful reintegration of that area into the legal and constitutional framework of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel didn't switch the microphone on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, can the document be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1803.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1803 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the Registrar call up document 3D00465, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Granic, in your testimony so far, you said several times that an agreement had been reached in Sector East with the rebel Serbs to open up roads or a road, namely, the Zagreb-Belgrade motorway. You also stated that there were certain problems in the implementation of the agreement on the part of rebel Serbs. Can you give us a few more points on that, by way of introduction to Operation Flash?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC
utterances.text: Before dealing with Operation Flash, it is important to say that the Z-4 plan, which had been worked on jointly by the ambassadors of the US, Russia, Germany, a plan which was not favorable for Croatia because, in fact, it provided Serbs with a state within a state. Croatia, regardless of the fact that it found it hard to accept it, did take part in negotiations for it, and discussing it; whereas, the rebel Serbs, Martic himself, refused to take the agreement -- to physically take it in his hand. The economic agreement which had been signed with the local Serbs, Serbs in general, not the ones in Krajina, was supposed to ensure the opening up of the Zagreb-Belgrade motorway. However, there were everyday incidents provoked -- provoked by them, nearly each and one of them had fatalities as their results. They wanted to make it clear, through these incidents, that the motorways was highly unsafe for use. This caused major discontent among the citizens of Croatia, as it showed them to be unreliable partners for any sort of economic, let alone political, settlement. They didn't want to discuss that one at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Under such circumstances where you say Croatia had to provide for an enormous number of refugees and was under heavy financial strain, the economy was an important part of its functioning, as it normally is, but especially under those circumstances. How significant, in that context, was the Zagreb-Belgrade motorway, and did it have to do with the bringing about of this agreement with the local Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC
utterances.text: It was very important, of course, for economic reasons. Both the railway lines Zagreb-Belgrade, Zagreb-Split were cut off, as well as the pipe -- as the oil pipeline. This caused enormous damage to Croatia. As in fact the closed Zagreb-Belgrade motorway did. This showed that the local Serbs did not want to seriously engage in any sort of talks, including the ones on economic matters, and it showed them that they were unreliable partners for any sort of dialogue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Under the circumstances following the discussions in the UN, and following the letters that you and President Tudjman sent, and following the signing of the economic agreement which failed, the military and police Operation Flash followed on the 3rd of May, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the Registrar call up 3D00465, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This is tab 7 in your binder, Mr. Granic. This is the message that president of the Republic of Croatia, Franjo Tudjman, addressed Croats and other citizens of the Republic of Croatia with on the 3rd of May, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we turn to page 3 of the document. 3D00465, we can see it on our screens. Page 3 of the document. [In English] The left side is accurate; but the right side is previous document, as I can see. Okay. It's okay now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this document, somewhere in the middle, the president says at the same time, as president of Croatia, I invite the Croatian Serbs to renounce those who are leading them and to accept the peaceful integration of the still occupied areas into the constitutional and legal and economic system of the democratic Republic of Croatia. The Croatian authorities guarantee the Serb ethnic community all the rights provided for by the Croatian constitution and the special constitutional law, in accordance with all international conventions. If they desist from armed resistance, Croatia will know how to establish its authority throughout its territory within its internationally recognised borders in the way this was done the day before yesterday and yesterday in Western Slavonia. Mr. Granic, we can see that President Tudjman, in this address of the general public, on the 3rd of May, 1995, called upon the Serb ethnic community to agree to a peaceful reintegration of that area into the Republic of Croatia. Is that the sort of state policy that you were part of at the time as a minister of -- as the minister of foreign affairs and -- what can you tell us on this message?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC
utterances.text: The military and police Operation Flash had as its primary role, or objective, the opening up of the Zagreb-Belgrade motorway. The second major goal was, once the first goal was achieved, was to liberate the occupied area and the so-called -- UNPA West. There had been no violations of human rights or international conventions. We had an excellent cooperation with all the institutions of the United Nations, with all the specialised agencies, such as the High Commissioner for Refugees, the ICRC. The cooperation we had was excellent. In short, over some 34 hours, over the period of some 34 hours, the operation was finished and it showed the resolution of the state to indicate that, unless it was able to do it so peacefully, it was able to ensure that the area was reintegrated into Croatia in -- in an armed way. However, at the same time, we hoped that this would be a warning to Martic and others to engage in serious talks with Croatia about a peaceful reintegration into Croatia. However, the response was that numerous cities, including Zagreb, were shelled. In Zagreb there was seven killed and 196 wounded, including as one of the targets the children's hospital Klaiceva, which I visited in the company of several ambassadors. We showed that what could immediately follow was a co-existence with the Serbs who remained through direct assistance and protection. Let me repeat that this operation did not meet with any objections from the international community, since I, as the minister of foreign affairs, visited, together with ambassadors, the relevant area, and I think it was precisely on the 3rd or on the 4th. I spoke to all the relevant foreign ministers from the neighbouring countries and the world at large. I explained the reason why the operation was carried out. There had been no pressure exerted from the international community on Croatia to speak of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I rise just to -- if we can check the interpretation at page 79, there's a sentence that starts on line 4 and continues on to line 5, I believe there's an adjective that was left out that might be important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Granic, if would you carefully listen, then I will read to you what appears on our transcript. And if there is any word missing which you'd like to bring in, please tell us. I read: "We had an excellent cooperation" -- is that the line?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The previous sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The previous sentence. I -- I again start reading: "There had been no violations of human rights or international conventions." Is there any word missing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were no serious violations of human rights or any violations of international conventions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So the word "serious" was missing. Please proceed, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation] Mr. Presiding Judge, I seek to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1804.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Granic, your diplomatic activity during the crisis period went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would next ask for 3D00497.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That is tab 9 in your binder. Thereby, you are responding to the Japanese Deputy Prime Minister, Mr. Kono. Could we move to page 2 of the letter, please. The penultimate paragraph where you say: "The Republic of Croatia still believes - and we shall persevere in this direction for as long as possible - that negotiations and peaceful resolution are the best way out of this crisis. We intend, for example, to turn Western Slavonia into a window of peaceful reintegration and to continue to fully cooperate with the international community at all its efforts aimed at bringing a just and lasting peace to south-east of Europe. But in order to continue with such policy, we need full understanding and support from the international community." Mr. Granic, first of all, do you recognise this letter of yours? Perhaps if we scroll up we may be able to see the signature. What type of contact with Mr. Kono was this?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC
utterances.text: He visited the Republic of Croatia. That was only one day preceding Operation Storm [as interpreted]. Of course, at that time, I could not mentioned the operation itself, because only during the next day, at the National Security Council meeting, the decision was made to undertake the operation. As I mentioned, that decision was made due to constant provocations and serious incidents resulting in a number of deaths. I believed it to be my duty to inform my colleague by rank, that is to say, the minister, Kono, about the operation, its reasons, its goals, and what we intended to do following that operation. We still believed that all indications were to the effect that the local Serbs would choose a rational way out, thereby choosing to seriously negotiate the political issues and peaceful reintegration into the legal system of the state of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel's microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you referred to the operation, Dr. Granic, which operation do have you in mind?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC
utterances.text: Operation Flash.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I say that, because in the transcript, page 81, line 22, it said Operation Storm. I believe Mr. Granic did not mention that. Hence, the correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Presiding Judge, I seek to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1805.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1805 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Could we please have 3D00503.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Granic, the diplomatic activity of Croatia was conducted via the president's office on the one hand, and on other hand, through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs; correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: At that time, Mr. Sarinic was around. What was his position?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC
utterances.text: He was the head of the President's office, and, as such, he was also tasked with communicating with the UN office in Zagreb, and he also had certain separate tasks during a certain period when he frequently -- or on several occasions met with Mr. Milosevic, when a peaceful solution to the conflict was sought in the area of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: On the screen, Dr. Granic, you see his letter sent on the 28th of June, 1995. It was sent to Mr. Yasushi Akashi. It is tab 11. He addresses Mr. Akashi by saying that, I quote: "With great surprise I received the answer which was ... sent by General Bernard Janvier, about you not having information on the entry of the army and heavy weaponry from SR Yugoslavia into occupied territories of the Republic of Croatia ..." Dr. Granic, what was the background to these events which caused Mr. Sarinic's letter to be sent? And you will see a follow-up letter from yourself as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel. I'm sorry to interrupt, but I think Mr. Mikulicic mistakenly said June 1995. It's July. Just so the witness can -- the letter is July 1995, and on line 10 of page 83, Mr. Mikulicic said June, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, we have obviously another problem with the translation, because I have the original in front of me, in Croatian language, where it states 28th of June, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We will ask the witness whether he can say something about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Granic, in the Croatian original that is before you, the date is the 28th of June. In the English translation made by the interpretation service -- the translation service of this Tribunal the date is 28th of July. Can you tell us the right date?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC
utterances.text: I'm quite positive that it was the 28th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us more about the background of these events.

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC
utterances.text: During that period of time, Milosevic sent General Mrksic to reorganise the army. There was heavy weaponry involved. They conducted exercises and stepped up military activity. They did not concede to any serious talks or negotiations but a peaceful reintegration. On the contrary, they stepped up their military activity. At that time, the Serbs from Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say, Karadzic's Serbs and Martic, were negotiating and making decisions on the creation of a common state. During that time the Serbs from Croatia actively participated in the encirclement of Bihac, and Belgrade offered its active assistance. Mr. Sarinic cautioned or tried to inform Mr. Akashi about the routes through which heavy weaponry was being introduced into the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And all that was happening in -- in, so to say, the face of the -- of UNPROFOR which was supposed to control the Croatian border?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC
utterances.text: That is completely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Presiding Judge, I seek to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1806.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1806 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Could we now please see the document 3D00495.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And that is tab 12 in your binder, Mr. Granic. On the same day, that is to say, the 28th of June, when Mr. Sarinic sent the letter to Mr. Akashi relating to the arrival of Serbian army and weapons to the occupied territory of Krajina, you also sent a letter but to the Secretary-General of United Nations, Mr. Boutros-Ghali, in which, on page 2 of this letter - if we could please see page 2 - you specified what were the high officers of the Yugoslav army who had crossed over to the occupied territory of the Republic of Croatia, including Colonel Slobodan Tarbuk. Then, Uros Despotovic and others. Tell us, what was your intention in sending Mr. Boutros-Ghali such a letter as this?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC
utterances.text: During Operation Flash and after it, we received documents which showed that all the soldiers of the so-called Republika Srpska were receiving salaries from Belgrade. So it was direct control from Belgrade. And at this point we also received information what were the new high officers which Belgrade had sent to the territory of Republika Srpska. We warned him, the Secretary-General of the United Nations, about the situation which was getting worse, and how the rebel Serbs were becoming more radical. And the new mandate of UNCRO was beginning, and practically at the same time, the rebel Serbs were obtaining new weapons, becoming radical. New top-ranking officers of the Yugoslav Army were coming to the territory of the Republic of Croatia, the territory of the so-called Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of this page, in the first paragraph, you note that this is a direct violation of the resolutions of the Security Council, because the soldiers are being transported with weapons across the border in Raca, since the 14th of June, 1995, and entering the occupied territories of Croatia at Dvor Na Uni? Please tell us, Mr. Granic, what was the reaction to this letter of yours?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC
utterances.text: There was no doubt that this letter was received with great concern. We know that the Secretary-General was concerned and, in particular, Mr. Akashi was concerned. Unfortunately, nothing specific was done. None of these soldiers were returned, no weapons were seized, so nothing happened. That is a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this document into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I took it, Mr. Waespi, that you wanted to say that you had no objections, which doesn't appear on the transcript. And on this assumption, Mr. Registrar, the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1807.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1807 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Granic, the whole situation, warning about the stepping up of the military forces in the so-called Krajina, in the occupied part of the Republic of Croatia, that was all connected with the situation around Bihac, in the neighbouring Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, around Bihac, but not only around it. I have to say that, at that time, a tragic event occurred which conditioned to a great extent our conduct, my own conduct, and the conduct of the Republic of Croatia, and it was the fall of Srebrenica, and I could say a few words about that too, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Granic, this Tribunal has heard a lot about the fall of Srebrenica and the tragic fate of Bosniaks until now --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So unless you insist on that, Mr. President, I think there is no need to discuss that event anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not see direct relevance to discuss in any further details the events of Srebrenica. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we should only note, Mr. Granic, Srebrenica was a protected UN zone, right?

utterances.speaker: MATE GRANIC
